paper.title: Maternal psychological distress and child psychosocial functioning in girls with central precocious puberty: a prospective study before and after GnRH analogue treatment.
paper.summary:
OBJECTIVES: Central precocious puberty (CPP) may have psychosocial implications for girls and their mothers. We evaluated changes in maternal psychological distress during gonadotropin-releasing hormone analogue (GnRHa) therapy and associations with child emotional, behavioral, and peer-related functioning.
METHODS: This prospective observational study included 40 girls with confirmed CPP and their mothers. Eligibility required documented progressive breast development before age 8, clinical progression, and biochemical central activation; isolated thelarche, isolated pubarche, and lipomastia were excluded. Child psychosocial measures and baseline maternal Depression Anxiety Stress Scale-21 (DASS-21) were completed at the same visit. Maternal DASS-21 was repeated at variable times during ongoing GnRHa therapy.
RESULTS: Mean total maternal DASS-21 score decreased from 13.38 ± 10.58 to 7.13 ± 8.15 (p<0.001). Maternal total DASS-21 showed moderate positive associations with total internalizing symptoms (ρ=0.501, p<0.001) and several RCADS-P domains; the total internalizing association remained after adjustment for BMI SDS (partial ρ=0.510, p<0.001). Among behavioral and social outcomes, maternal total DASS-21 was associated with hyperactivity, while exploratory maternal anxiety analyses showed associations with the ADHD Index and hyperactivity. DASS-21 change was not associated with age at diagnosis or reassessment interval.
CONCLUSIONS: Maternal psychological distress decreased over time during GnRHa therapy and showed moderate associations with mother-reported emotional symptoms in girls with confirmed CPP. These findings support individualized, family-centered psychosocial assessment as part of CPP care.

paper.title: Neuromelanin-inspired metal-selenomelanin nanonetworks restore neuronal excitability in radiation-induced brain injury.
paper.summary: Radiation-induced brain injury (RIBI) affects up to 30% of patients receiving cranial radiotherapy, representing an irreversible complication lacking effective therapies. Research advances are limited by poor blood-brain barrier drug penetration and overreliance on ex vivo pathology, which cannot resolve dynamic neuronal dysfunction. Inspired by neuromelanin, we fabricated metal-selenomelanin nanonetworks (MSMNs), combined with in vivo electrophysiology to investigate and mitigate radiation-triggered neural dysfunction. In 6-gray whole body-irradiated mice, MSMN normalized neuronal excitability and restored medium spiny neuron firing and striatal circuit activity, improving locomotor and anxiety-related behaviors. Besides central functional recovery, MSMN provides systemic radioprotection, ensuring full 30-day survival, protecting radiosensitive organs and facilitating hematopoietic recovery. This work identifies neuronal excitability as an underexplored therapeutic target for RIBI, establishing neuromelanin-mimetic selenomelanin nanonetworks as a bioinspired platform linking molecular radioprotection to circuit-level restoration for radiation-induced neurological injury.

paper.title: Sound context modulates perceived vocal emotion
paper.summary:
Abstract
                Many animal vocalizations contain nonlinear acoustic phenomena as a consequence of physiological arousal. In humans, nonlinear features are processed early in the auditory system, and are used to efficiently detect alarm calls and other urgent signals. Yet, high-level emotional and semantic contextual factors likely guide the perception and evaluation of roughness features in vocal sounds. Here we examined the relationship between perceived vocal arousal and auditory context. We presented listeners with nonverbal vocalizations (yells of a single vowel) at varying levels of portrayed vocal arousal, in two musical contexts (clean guitar, distorted guitar) and one non-musical context (modulated noise). As predicted, vocalizations with higher levels of portrayed vocal arousal were judged as more negative and more emotionally aroused than the same voices produced with low vocal arousal. Moreover, both the perceived valence and emotional arousal of vocalizations were significantly affected by both musical and non-musical contexts. These results show the importance of auditory context in judging emotional arousal and valence in voices and music, and suggest that nonlinear features in music are processed similarly to communicative vocal signals.

paper.title: The experience of time: neural mechanisms and the interplay of emotion, cognition and embodiment
paper.summary:
Time research has been a neglected topic in the cognitive neurosciences of the last decades: how do humans perceive time? How and where in the brain is time processed? This introductory paper provides an overview of the empirical and theoretical papers on the psychological and neural basis of time perception collected in this theme issue. Contributors from the fields of cognitive psychology, psychiatry, neurology and neuroanatomy tackle this complex question with a variety of techniques ranging from psychophysical and behavioural experiments to pharmacological interventions and functional neuroimaging. Several (and some new) models of
                    how
                    and
                    where
                    in the brain time is processed are presented in this unique collection of recent research that covers experienced time intervals from milliseconds to minutes. We hope this volume to be conducive in developing a better understanding of the sense of time as part of complex set of brain–body factors that include cognitive, emotional and body states.

paper.title: Motivation, Emotion, Learning Experience, and Second Language Comprehensibility Development in Classroom Settings: A Cross‐Sectional and Longitudinal Study
paper.summary:
Abstract
                  
                    
                    This study presents a cross‐sectional and longitudinal analysis of how 108 high school students in English as a foreign language (EFL) classrooms enhanced the comprehensibility of their second language (L2) speech according to different motivation, emotion, and experience profiles. Students’ learning patterns were primarily associated with their emotional states (anxiety vs. enjoyment) and secondarily with their motivational dispositions (clear vision of ideal future selves). Students’ anxiety together with weaker Ideal L2 Self related negatively to their performance at the beginning of the project—performance that they had achieved after several years of EFL instruction. Students’ enjoyment together with greater Ideal L2 Self predicted the extent to which they practiced and developed their L2 speech within the 3‐month framework of the project. Results suggest that more frequent L2 use with positive emotions directly impacts acquisition, which may in turn lead to the lessening of negative emotions and better long‐term L2 comprehensibility.
